article_text:
Il libro di Umico Niwa , Daphne , è pieno di istantanee, di piccole installazioni, di lavori artistici vari, ma anche di oggetti casuali, come un mazzo di fiori, peluche che sembrano quasi aver vissuto troppe vite, qualche animale ripreso qua e là, molta natura e diverse persone che l’artista ha ritenuto importante inserire. Si tratta di una raccolta intima, intervallata da poesie scritte da Umico stessa, il cui titolo riprende volutamente la figura dell’omonima ninfa della mitologia greca.

Una costruzione che ripercorre a ritroso la sua vita e il concetto di cambiamento inteso come trasformazione e rigenerazione, visibile anche in Daphne, Act Two , la nuova mostra dell’artista visitabile nella galleria romana T293. Articolata in due grandi stanze, la personale prolunga l’evoluzione invocata e celebrata nei progetti collaterali, a partire dallo spazio iniziale Act One , in cui sono posizionate figure composte da materiali organici e peltro, fino al secondo perimetro Act Two , dove i soggetti, i Daphnes (così vengono chiamati anche nel testo critico), interagiscono l’uno con l’altro.

Le composizioni esposte in mostra si pongono in continuità con i lavori precedenti dell’artista: ramoscelli con fiori d’ogni genere riposti in luoghi distanti da quello naturale, in prossimità di una presa, su un microonde, in un appartamento, come piante rampicanti attorno ad un tubo, oppure emergenti tra contatori e lampade appese al soffitto.

La natura scelta non è uguale a se stessa, è multiforme, estremamente colorata e, in certi casi bruciata, a tratti essiccata, senza tuttavia mai dare l’idea di essere priva di vita o ormai da buttare. D’altronde i Daphnes , che appaiono come personaggi di una commedia teatrale, sono, per Umico, anche strumento per affrontare un’esperienza personale, come lo è stata la transizione sessuale, con grande profondità, riconoscendo l’importanza di prestare ascolto alle nuove generazioni a dispetto del moltiplicarsi di episodi di violenza, alimentati, in buona parte, dall’avanzamento di politiche regressive in diversi Paesi del mondo. Con la personale e prima ancora con il libro, Umico ricorda il giorno dell’intervento e il delicato tema del post-operatorio che trovano sfogo nella realtà scenica di Daphne, Act Two . Il corpo assume così una funzione di collante tra gli elementi, i Daphnes, e l’evoluzione dell’ambiente circostante. Chi partecipa al “gioco” può agire dall’interno, in una condizione fittizia, interferendo con la rappresentazione di uno luogo e di un tempo irreali. Daphne ritorna proprio in questa prospettiva. Nel suo libro Umico ricorda il momento in cui è nata la serie, ossia quando, dopo essersi imbattuta in una statua raffigurante la ninfa, ha sentito il bisogno di fondere il metallo nello stampo di un ramo, e ricorda come ciò stesse accadendo in un periodo complesso in cui stava affrontando “the loss of having children of my own, witnessing the death of a tree, and the passing of another transwoman in my community. Daphne was there for me when I needed the most”.

I Daphne fanno così da collante, e i germogli che Umico innesta in luoghi urbani e spesso al chiuso lasciano, senza retorica, una sensazione di attesa, in parte di speranza, sebbene al contempo colgano quel senso di disperazione iniziale richiamato e semplificato nei resti visibili agli angoli delle grandi stanze della galleria. L’evoluzione si presenta come un processo fragile ma ostinato, mentre emerge una trasformazione sufficiente a interrompere le tracce dell’incertezza nell’ambiente. Significativa, in questo senso, è una poesia inserita nel libro, che recita “If I could cast a ripple through space and time, so as to hold you both, see you once more”, un’espressione del desiderio, del superamento dei limiti imposti dallo spazio e dal tempo, se non anche una metafora della memoria e del legame con ciò che è stato, un nuovo significato di evoluzione, un senso più ampio di espansione e, al contempo, il legame chiaro e limpido con la versione passata della propria vita.

The gallerist who would be paying him for this, if she decided to spend what he was asking, sat between them as they chatted, interrupting their rapport from time to time to underline the parts of the artist’s life that she felt were important art historically. Every summer Jonah compiled a list of about a hundred upcoming museum shows for the newspaper’s special fall preview section. The first time he did it they were visiting Nadia’s college friend at her parents’ house in Pasadena, where he had to share a queen-size bed with Nadia and eight-month-old Orly. Fording hundreds of press releases, making decisions, and writing one-to-two-sentence synopses of complex shows he hadn’t seen while exhausted and sleepless was a trial. But the next year found him more confident, and ultimately the process became so automatic that it made no impression on him at all. If someone asked him in August, after he had filed his piece, what fall shows he was looking forward to, he would have to refer back to the document to come up with an answer.

One exhibit that did stick in his mind, though, the year Orly was six, was of a famous Chinese ink painting, a still life of persimmons, making a brief visit to the Asian Art Museum in San Francisco. It would be coming from the Japanese monastery which had acquired it when it was already nearly 300 years old and which had then kept it mostly rolled up and hidden away since the early 1500s. Jonah mentioned the show to his editor as one he’d like to cover, emphasising how unprecedented it was for the piece to travel and reminding her that he was her only freelancer with any affinity for, or knowledge of, Asian art.

She was amenable to his writing about it, she told him, but said that, because of the expense of covering the war in Ukraine, the art section had no travel budget left for the year.

“Do you really have to see it in person?” she asked.

Jonah hesitated.

“I mean,” he said, “for a review.”

Then cannily, or guilelessly, he added that he planned to go see it regardless. He figured that after more than a decade as an art critic, it was time to admit that art was important to him, and that so long as she did pay him to write something, he would at least break even on the experience. She offered to pay for a night in a hotel and he replied that he was planning to stay with his cousin.

“Well,” she said noncommittally, “see if you can find a cheap flight.”

Using credit card points, he found one for a couple of hundred dollars. He checked with his cousin and made plans to stay for two nights; it would be the longest he had been alone since Orly was born. Then he forgot about it, mostly. But he would mention his upcoming trip now and then to this or that person, amused to cut the figure of an adult whose job let him travel. Downtown to take notes about a conceptual art show, he met his father for coffee.

“Wow!” Alan exclaimed when Jonah told him about the ink painting. “I always wanted to see that but your mother and I were never in Kyoto on the right day.”

When the time came to go and Jonah found himself alone with a backpack on the E train, bound for Kennedy Airport, he was bemused again. As a younger man, he had travelled to escape his ordinary life, to fling himself without boundaries into unfamiliar locales. His last visit to San Francisco had been to visit a girl he’d briefly dated in New York, and he could still summon up the Pacific smell of the air when he first stepped out of the airport, the dark luxury of the apartment she was borrowing, the softness of her freckled, paper-white skin as they made love and fell asleep in a narrow guest-room bed. She had reminded him of a doe. Now, as he passed through the airport security line in New York, endured a two-hour delay caused by San Francisco air traffic related to the upcoming Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation conference, read the London Review of Books, crammed himself into an economy seat, watched half a movie on his iPad, and took a cab, at his cousin’s suggestion, to Bernal Heights, it all felt more like an errand, albeit a pleasant one, than an adventure. The air smelled of nothing. His own company felt like a childhood friend he was glad to see again, but with whom, because it had been so long, he felt shy.

First thing the following morning, Jonah accompanied his cousin, an accomplished video game designer, as he walked his dog in a nearby park. They hadn’t met in years, and Jonah felt shy with him, too — as well as rebuked in his own aimless financial irresponsibility by the cousin’s comfortably furnished 3-bedroom house with basement rental apartment attached. Looking for something to talk about, he asked whether there had been many protests about Israel’s response to the attacks of October 7.

“Not really,” his cousin said. “I did drive past one group of people with signs that said ‘Stop the Genocide.’”

His tone made clear what he thought of the protestors’ use of the word “genocide.” Not seeing any benefit in starting an argument with his host at 7:30 in the morning, Jonah changed the subject. He went and climbed a nearby hill for its view of the city; returned to the house, where his cousin fed him breakfast; and rode the bus to a still awakening Chinatown to see a show someone had told him about, work by an artist he liked at a gallery he had encountered at art fairs but never visited in person. He chatted with the young man behind the desk, asking what else there was to see in the neighbourhood and sharing his concern that the artist, a Native American ceramicist who had gotten very popular, might get boxed into grinding out the same thing over and over. Because the young man asked, Jonah also shared his name. There was a photography gallery a few blocks away, another one Jonah knew by reputation; walking there he saw a large protest of the summit that had delayed his flight.

He got past the desk and into the show — tasteful, boring photography by a successful Japanese artist, what he privately thought of as “rich people art” — with only a brief hello, but then turned around, just when he would have walked out again, to see that the gallery founder and two directors had emerged to greet him.

“They told us you were coming,” explained one of the directors, a pretty young woman in a severe business suit. Once the founder had shaken his hand and gone back to his office, Jonah let the pretty young director show him around the exhibit he’d already dismissed as well as the gallery’s back office and viewing room. He took his usual approach in such situations, making small talk as if at a cocktail party and biding his time. He admired the unique design of the display racks in the viewing room. He inquired after her family and asked where she liked to eat in the neighbourhood. As soon as he could he slipped out and hurried over to City Lights, where he bought two paperbacks by the Sicilian writer Leonardo Sciascia, whom he’d never read before.

The restaurant she recommended turned out to be an ornate Szechuan spot, deserted at that hour, whose prices he could not possibly afford. Slinking out again after looking at the menu he felt foolish to have expected anything else. Fortunately he’d overheard the clerk at City Lights mention another place, an old-school Hunanese lunch counter where there was a television playing the local news and they did not offend Jonah’s sensibilities by charging for tea. Later he rode out to the Berkeley Art Museum and Pacific Film Archive to see the exhibition of a grad school friend, another conceptual artist who made work about North American settler colonialism; the next morning, he visited a sculptor who had gone to college with Nadia and had just spent six months carving the impurities out of an enormous chunk of quartz salvaged from a commercial rock quarry.

This sculptor’s New York gallery had just closed and he had a new baby in a carrier on his chest. Jonah’s heart was in his mouth every time the sculptor leaned over his opus, bringing the baby’s head within an inch of a corner; he remembered the dirty looks he used to get from old women in Jackson Heights when they saw him carrying his own newborn infant under one arm like a football. He and the sculptor went out for dim sum and to a bookstore and the sculptor shared the advice another artist had given him about making money.

“‘Use archival material,’” he said, “‘and get used to doing the same thing over and over.’”

Then Jonah walked a mile and a half to the Asian Art Museum, which had been closed to the public to host a grand lunch for the spouses of the heads of state in town for APEC.

“Jill Biden was standing right here two hours ago,” the museum’s press chief told him, grinning and squeezing his arm, once he’d gotten past security and been led into the dim and empty gallery. “I’ll leave you alone.”

Publicists liked to talk, and curators liked to lecture, but Jonah had learned to be forthright about his need for solitude. This time they had agreed ahead of time that he would have 45 minutes to himself before the curator arrived to explain what he was supposed to think of the painting. When he was starting out, he had sometimes spent many hours over multiple days confronting a work that perplexed him. In this case, having already seen many images of what turned out to be a very easily photographed black and white art work, and having already begun to write down ideas earlier in the day, he could probably have made do with a glance. He was unlikely to experience any transcendence in such a tightly choreographed encounter, anyway. He was just too contrary. But showing up felt like a matter of principle, and after all, it couldn’t hurt.

When the press contact, a former dancer type who later surprised Jonah by mentioning his wife and two children, returned with the curator, a trim older woman in an embroidered jacket, Jonah prepared to joust. She was perfectly nice and had interesting things to say. But he needed her to understand that he was no mere journalist, to whom the Zen esthetic was news, while she, as an academic, had to demonstrate her mastery of the material. Once he felt they had both made their points, he looked at his watch, and they continued next door to a Japanese pop art exhibit. Then the curator excused herself, but the former dancer offered Jonah a tour of the rest of the museum, and Jonah couldn’t see how to refuse, even though his feet hurt and his eyes were exhausted. He hadn’t ever been there before and, as the dancer pointed out, there was no way of knowing if he’d ever be back.

When finally he left, with many thanks and professions of good will, he got on a train to a gentrified section of Oakland for dinner with a close college friend who had, after an interval in academia, become a corporate lawyer. Jonah held the friend’s new baby and then, leaving the baby and his older brother with either the night nurse or the mother in law — she wasn’t introduced — he, his friend, and his friend’s wife, also a corporate lawyer, walked to a nearby French restaurant. Jonah had been surprised, because his friend always seemed worried about money, by how nice his house was, but he supposed it made sense. The first thing his friend said, once they had been seated and had ordered some appetizers, was, “Flying across the country to see one painting is completely ridiculous.”

Jonah wasn’t sure whether he was meant to litigate this question, for entertainment’s sake, or to agree that he had wandered into an unbelievable life. He suspected the latter, but either way he didn’t feel up to it.

“Well,” he said mildly, “art is important to some people.”

“No, of course,” his friend replied, and Jonah stopped listening. In the morning he discovered that a train ran directly to the airport from quite close to his cousin’s house. There had been no reason to take a cab when he arrived. He began transcribing his notes on the airplane, and then began writing, and when this flight, too, was delayed, and they were all forced to deplane for several hours, he was delighted. The airline gave them food vouchers, there was a decent enough sushi counter, and this way he could finish his piece and finish watching Parasite on his iPad before returning to family life. It was a beautiful experience. He was engaged in what he was doing, but with something deeper than his anxious ordinary mind; he could feel himself pirouette around the ink painting’s formal qualities and Buddhist subtext like an ice skater. “The point of this minimalism isn’t to make anything simple,” he concluded, after about 1000 words, “but to cut away distractions and reveal how complicated the world actually is.”

He filed that evening from Kennedy Airport, and when there was no reply the following day, he wondered if he should call. But then the assistant art editor sent an edit, and he dared hope he could get through the whole process without talking on the phone at all. He did end up speaking to the assistant editor, because she would need a synopsis of his piece for a meeting the following week and called to ask him to write one for her. In the course of their exchange, he mentioned that some people called “Six Persimmons” the “Zen Mona Lisa.” She suggested putting this phrase in the subheadline, and to make this intelligible, he agreed to add the fact that some people called “Six Persimmons” the “Zen Mona Lisa” to his story.

When the piece was published, he got vastly more response than he usually did, which is to say that as many as three or four people emailed him about it. One was a former college professor, who said that he wasn’t sure either of them had brought their best to the class they had shared, but that he congratulated Jonah on conserving his energies for such top-flight art writing. The next week Jonah went to Chinatown to visit an artist he might profile for a museum catalogue, a renowned older Japanese woman who had lived like a squatter in an unfurnished loft for 40 years. The gallerist who would be paying him for this, if she decided to spend what he was asking, sat between them as they chatted, interrupting their rapport from time to time to underline the parts of the artist’s life that she felt were important art historically. When she got up to use the bathroom, the artist followed her with her eyes.

“She’s okay,” the artist said. “But I think something weird about her. Like whenever we travel, she insist on getting one room with king size bed.”

“To share?” Jonah exclaimed.

On his way to Tribeca, where he was meeting his father for coffee, Jonah ran into a different art dealer, the one whose conceptual art show he had just reviewed, and she invited him into her office for a chat. They talked about marriage and their children, as they usually did, and she thanked him for the review, which he shrugged off.

“No,” she said, “it’s huge.”

She had worked at a mega gallery before opening her own space, and she told him that reviews in his paper had been the only ones the mega gallerist cared about. They appeared in sales presentations. They played a key role in what she called the mega gallerist’s “ongoing pissing contest” with his peers.

“Yeah,” Jonah laughed, “and then I get $250.”

The dealer’s jaw dropped, and he in turn stared right back at her. He couldn’t remember having ever surprised her before.

“Yeah,” he repeated. “Two-fifty for the short ones.”

“But you have so much power!” she exclaimed.

He didn’t know what to say.

“How was the piece?” Alan asked him, once they were sitting side by side in the little cafe that now occupied the former boarding house where Frederick Douglass had first slept when he came to New York.

“To be honest,” Jonah said, “I think it comes through pretty well in reproduction.” He made a deprecating gesture. “You know, it’s black and white.”

“It’s still good you went,” Alan said.

“Oh, yeah, no,” Jonah said, “it was a great trip. I’m glad I went.”

He walked Alan back to the loft and went upstairs to say hello to his mother, to whom he couldn’t help boasting that he’d gotten some nice emails about his latest review.

“Oh, I’m so glad!” she exclaimed. “Because I saw someone on Facebook making fun of you for calling it the Zen Mona Lisa.”
excerpt_original: A review of an ancient Chinese ink painting takes an art critic on a journey through his own past.

article_text:
Tree Week: Venessa Monokian: As the Glow Grows

©Venessa Monokian, Installation Box

Venessa Monokian initially used photography as a tool for coping with the limitations of her learning disability. She used it as an alternative way of understanding the world, and began experimenting with different ways of presenting images. Monokian photographed the tropical foliage of her home in Florida, and continued that practice after moving to Houston. She has expanded her process beyond the traditional flat image, and began cutting and shaping her pictures into sculptural forms. Shadows add depth to the work and the viewer is now aware of the photo as physical object. Monokian’s work questions the definition of a photograph, and peaks the curiosity of the viewer so that they move closer to explore the many facets of her images.

©Venessa Monokian, Installation Box

Venessa Monokian is an artist whose work investigates ideas about her environment, extending beyond the tangible to explore the psychological and emotional elements of space. The viewer’s physical interaction with her pieces is integral to the final experience, fostering a dynamic partnership between the artist, the work, and the audience.

Recent projects in 2026 include an artist book exhibition at Cornell University, a two-person exhibition with the Throughline, and most recently a solo exhibition at the Houston Center for Photography. In 2025, her work was part of CraftTexas at the Houston Center for Contemporary Craft, and she participated in an Instagram takeover for the Magenta Foundation (Canada).

In 2024, she received the Jones Artist Award from the Houston Endowment for the Arts. Based in Houston, Monokian is affiliated with Box13 ArtSpace and the Throughline Collective. She holds an MFA from Florida International University and is originally from Miami. Her work has been exhibited internationally at venues including Met/Gal (Austin), the Contemporary Arts Center (New Orleans), Mac Fine Art (Fort Lauderdale), the Academy of Fine Arts in Poland, and Panal 361 in Argentina.

Instagram: @vmonokian

©Venessa Monokian, Installation Box

Q: What led you to begin work as a photographer? Do you also work in other mediums? Do you create sculpture with things other than your photographs?

I actually have a learning disability, and growing up I didn’t always fully understand how to grasp or communicate how I visually see the world around me. Photography became an alternative way for me to better understand both the physical and optical aspects of looking, as well as the emotional and conceptual ways we formulate our understanding of the world around us.

Being able to easily access and digest medical or pedagogical journals and other written information was a struggle for me, so I began using photography as an adaptive learning tool for myself.

Over time, that process has expanded beyond traditional photography. I am interested in experimenting with different materials and ways of presenting photographic information, including cutting, sculptural installation, color, and more recently, interactive video. For me, the medium is a tool for exploring ideas rather than something I feel limited to.

©Venessa Monokian, Drip

Q: Your images seem to be taken mostly of tropical plants. Is there something that you find fascinating about their foliage?

I was raised in South Florida, so the tropics are naturally a major influence on my work. But the particular plant I am photographing also affects the place I call home now in Houston. It became interesting to me to use this particular plant called air potato vine (Dioscorea bulbifera) as a way of connecting my two home spaces.

The plant is an invasive species that was brought to South Florida and has taken over and completely altered parts of that environment. In some places, it has changed the landscape so much that it no longer looks like the place I remember from my childhood.

At the same time, this plant is being sold in Houston as a decorative plant and is beginning to affect the ecosystem of my new home. So I am taking the knowledge and experiences I have from Miami and using them as a way to share and explore these ideas with people in Houston and beyond.

The plant becomes a way for me to talk about more than ecology. It becomes a connection between two places I call home and a way of thinking about how our relationships with nature change as we move through different environments.

©Venessa Monokian, Engulfed

Q:What led you to begin cutting your photographs?

I actually started cutting photographs before this current body of work, when I knew I was going to need to leave South Florida. Miami is my home forever and will always be in my heart, but it is very expensive and difficult for an artist and educator to sustain a life there.

I was trying to think of a body of work that I could develop as I moved from place to place. The idea was to photograph my surroundings and isolate the plants I found, using this approach to learn more about the native flora and fauna of wherever I was living.

It wasn’t until later that the air potato vine in particular came into the work. That developed once I found my new home in Houston and realized that this same plant was present here, creating an unexpected connection between the two places.

©Venessa Monokian, In Knots 11

Q: Once they are cut, you shape them into sculptural pieces. What led you to do that, and how does displaying them in 3D change the viewer’s experience?

I was on a residency in Argentina and, at the time, was creating work that predated this current body of work. I was cutting the photographs intricately and layering them to create 3D environments, more similar to a tunnel book.

However, I didn’t have enough work by the end of my residency to fill the gallery space. So I separated the layered works into individual panels, and that is when I started noticing the shadows and really loved the interplay between the positive and negative spaces.

Once I got back home and pinned the work up to study it, the humidity started to affect the photographs, making them bend and shape in interesting ways. I found this much more interesting to see, so I began to intentionally cut and shape the works.

The shift into three-dimensional work also changed the relationship between the photograph and the viewer. Instead of simply looking at an image, the viewer becomes aware of the physical object, its depth, its shadows, and the space around it.

©Venessa Monokian, Small-in-Knots 03

Q: The sculptural pieces seem to have a reddish glow coming from behind. Can you explain how you achieved this, and how it adds to the experience?

I was thinking about how I could highlight the areas of the images where the air potato was located, and the idea of painting the back of the cut photographs in those isolated areas emerged.

The hope is that I can use these different techniques and approaches to entice the viewer and make them more curious to ask questions. Is this a photograph? Where is the light coming from? Is this a real plant? Where is it from?

Those questions and that curiosity lead someone to look for answers, much like my own curiosity about better understanding my learning disability, my environment, and the world around me led me to explore and make this work.

I like the idea that the work doesn’t necessarily give you all the answers. Instead, it creates enough curiosity to make you want to look closer and investigate.

©Venessa Monokian, Small-in-Knots 04

Q: You do not add any protective coating to the paper sculptures, which allows the material to remain responsive and vulnerable rather than completely controlled or protected. Can you explain your reason for this?

I am really leaning into the fragility of the paper. When temperature or humidity varies, the work begins to curl and undulate on its own, and I find this organic response to the space really interesting. Once deinstalled, it generally returns to its normal shape.

©Venessa Monokian, Small-in-Knots 07

Q: Is there anything else you would like to tell us about your work?

My hope is that the work empowers me to explore these topics and, in turn, encourages others to have conversations about them. I think it is important to have dialogue with one another, to ask questions, and to remain open to learning.

For me, the work isn’t about having all the answers. It is about being curious, asking questions, and creating opportunities for other people to do the same.

©Venessa Monokian, Small-in-Knots 08

article_text:
James Gunn has once again taken to Threads in defense of his DC universe, and this time, is clarifying his previously proposed eight- to 10-year roadmap for the fictional world and making it clearer where each character stands within it.

“You can look at my quotes from January ’23 when we started and I said we were going to do exactly what we’re doing,” the DC Studios co-head wrote responding to a now-deleted post. “I said some stories would be standalone like the Guardians movies were (which is what Clayface is) and some stories would have part of a larger narrative structure, which is what the Superman Saga is. All that said, each piece of the larger story should work on its own with or without having to see everything else.”

Related Stories

Jonathan Bailey and Natalie Portman Thriller 'Pumping Black' Adds Daniel Quinn-Toye, Lucas Lynggaard Tønnesen, Arieh Worthalter and Tony Hale (EXCLUSIVE)

He continued in a second post: “ALSO, some things get conflated here. The often cited ‘8 to 10 year roadmap’ originally pitched wasn’t only story points (although that was a part of it), but also the plan for DC as a whole, including focusing on diamond characters (Superman, Batman , WW) as well as smaller characters we could turn into diamonds (Krypto, John Stewart, Peacemaker), how we would foster filmmaker freedom & allow for multiple tones & ratings, the influences of Star Wars & George RR Martin, and so much more.”

Gunn’s note about the “8 to 10 year roadmap” refers to his and fellow co-head Peter Safran’s 2022 remarks during a virtual Warner Bros. Discovery town hall, during which he’d said they’d mapped out an 8- to ten-year plan for DC. In a third post, he added: “It’s exciting seeing things START to come together and all that makes me even more excited for what we have in store for everyone in Man of Tomorrow.”

On Saturday, Gunn took to the social media platform to defend his decision to expand the DC universe with “individual stories” amid criticism that his films aren’t building toward a major crossover event.

Responding to a commenter who pointed out that Gunn doesn’t necessarily need to lay the foundation for one totally interconnected universe, he wrote, “I couldn’t agree more.” “DCU is just an alternate universe; we can enter at any location or time and tell THAT story. I dislike the idea that individual stories aren’t meaningful unless they lead to something else. People not understanding this is strange to me, because ‘Star Wars’ has essentially been doing this for 50 years across movies, shows, games and books, admittedly without the tonal variety,” he wrote.

Gunn’s next film, “ Superman: Man of Tomorrow ,” hits theaters July 9, 2027.

article_text:
Listeners might know John Early as a (very funny) comedian, actor, Toni Collette–superfan, and more—but last year at the Toronto International Film Festival, he debuted a new role: auteur. His directorial debut, Maddie’s Secret , takes cues from TV movies, PSAs, erotic thrillers, internet videos, Paul Verhoeven’s Showgirls , and other high-low cultural touchstones to craft a movie that, despite all these influences and parodic touches, feels wonderfully original and earnest. Early plays the titular Maddie, a food influencer who struggles with bulimia, with sincere commitment, somehow walking the tightrope between camp, laugh-out-loud wit, and a profound empathy.

Maddie’s Secret opens in cinemas on June 19. Keep your ears open for Part 2 of this conversation, which will be dropping soon as an exclusive for Film Comment subscribers.
excerpt_original: The comedian and actor discusses his directorial debut, a wonderfully original send-up of TV movies, erotic thrillers, and more

article_text:
C’est une lettre détaillée, adressée à la communauté internationale dans Variety , qui exsude l’inquiétude. Le 10 octobre dernier, plusieurs dizaines de professionnels du cinéma brésiliens ont appelé à porter « une grande attention au second tour de l’élection présidentielle » , le 25 octobre. Le scrutin, qui oppose le président sortant Lula au candidat d’extrême droite Flávio Bolsonaro, fils de l’ancien chef d’État Jair Bolsonaro (aujourd’hui condamné à 27 ans de prison pour coup d’État), est extrêmement serré. Et une victoire du second constituerait une menace non seulement pour l’industrie audiovisuelle, mais aussi pour l’ensemble des institutions démocratiques.

Parmi les signataires , Kleber Mendonça Filho, réalisateur de L’Agent secret , l’acteur principal du film Wagner Moura, mais aussi le producteur de Je suis toujours là, Rodrigo Teixeira, le cinéaste Karim Aïnouz, ou encore l’actrice Alice Braga. Flávio Bolsonaro ne leur a pas directement répondu, mais le candidat d’extrême droite a appelé « les artistes de droite » à le soutenir .

Si le cinéma brésilien connaît un renouveau sur la scène internationale, avec une moisson de prix dans les plus grandes cérémonies ces deux dernières années ( Je suis toujours là, sacré meilleur film étranger aux Oscars, Wagner Moura couronné à Cannes 2025 et aux Golden Globes), c’est notamment grâce à la politique culturelle volontariste du président Lula, revenu au pouvoir il y a trois ans. Flávio Bolsonaro, arrivé en tête au premier tour de l’élection avec 47,03% des voix (contre 45,16% pour Lula), promet de couper net les subventions et l’industrie dans son élan, en menant une politique austéritaire similaire à celle entreprise par son père. Entre 2019 et 2023, Jair Bolsonaro avait notamment amputé les budgets de l’agence nationale du cinéma et du Fonds pour le secteur audiovisuel de près de 43%.

▌ À LIRE AUSSI

Maud Chirio, historienne : « Le film de Walter Salles est très habile sur le plan de la bataille mémorielle. »

Avec l’élection de son fils, le septième art pourrait en outre devenir un instrument de propagande. Flávio Bolsonaro est en effet sous le coup d’une enquête pour détournements de fonds publics, car il aurait alloué une partie de ses indemnités parlementaires au financement de Dark Horse , un biopic encore inédit à la gloire… de son propre père. Aux manettes du projet tourné en anglais, on retrouve le réalisateur Cyrus Nowrasteh et l’acteur Jim Caviezel, figures de proue du cinéma évangélique américain.

INGÉRENCES AMÉRICAINES

Cet intérêt de l’Amérique ultra-conservatrice pour la politique brésilienne ne s’arrête pas à la production de films douteux. Les signataires de la lettre ouverte rappellent que les signes d’ingérence des États-Unis dans l’élection se multiplient. Dans une enquête glaçante, deux journalistes du Guardian ont montré comment l’administration Trump détourne les fonds du Département d’État américain normalement utilisés pour la défense des droits humains, et les redirige vers des groupes anti-communistes, anti-immigration, ou en faveur des droits des minorités blanches en Afrique. Un million de dollars a spécifiquement été alloué à un programme visant à affaiblir la Cour suprême brésilienne, à l’origine de la condamnation de Jair Bolsonaro.

Dans le même temps, « plusieurs observateurs ont soulevé un risque d’asymétrie dans la diffusion des contenus politiques » sur les réseaux sociaux, rappellent les signataires de la lettre ouverte. Le groupe Meta, qui détient Instagram et Facebook, est soupçonné d’entraver les publications de Lula et ses soutiens. Ce que l’entreprise dément , invoquant des « problèmes techniques » .

C’est dans le contexte de ces ingérences étrangères répétées, alors que l’industrie se relève à peine des années Jair Bolsonaro et que son fils promet de réécrire la Constitution du pays, que le cinéma brésilien s’alarme d’un retour en arrière. « Protéger la liberté d’expression et assurer la viabilité à long terme de l’industrie audiovisuelle brésilienne est indissociable de la défense de la démocratie , assurent les signataires de la lettre ouverte. Nous appelons la presse internationale à couvrir rigoureusement le processus électoral, et les institutions concernées à enquêter sur tous ces soupçons de façon indépendante. »
